title: The Protestants mean only that nothing good precedes justifying faith
source_text: LIV. Sed manifestum est ex iis quae superius exposita fuerunt, Protestantes quum docent, quicquid fit ante justificationem non bonum opus, sed peccatum esse, & cum Augustino dicunt bona opera non praecedere justificandum, sed sequi justificatum, non aliud sibi velle, quam nihil omnino boni fieri posse ante fidem Justificantem, & eos sub justificatione complecti ipsam fidem per quam justificamur: adeoque tum pro eodem habere, bona opera fieri ante justificationem, & fieri ab eo qui adhuc infidelis est. Caeterum, si quis justificationem distinguat ab ipsa fide justificante, & sumat illam praecise pro peccatoris absolutione, & peccatorum ejus remissione, Protestantes eosdem non inficiari quin boni quidam actus, & opera quae Deo placeant, antecedant nostram justificationem. Qualis est in primis ipse actus fidei quae justificat impium, perfugium peccatoris ad Dei misericordiam, dolor de peccatis praeteritis & eorum detestatio, propositum novae vitae, Imploratio divinae gratiae, spes veniae obtinendae & actus alii similes, qui prius natura in homine existant, quam peccata illi remissa sint, & priusquam haberi possit pro justificato.
pass_a_gloss: LIV. But it is manifest from those things which were set out above, that the Protestants when they teach, that whatever is done before justification is not a good work, but sin, and with Augustine say that good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the justified, mean nothing else, than that nothing at all good can be done before Justifying faith, and that they embrace under justification the very faith through which we are justified: and so then hold for the same, that good works be done before justification, and be done by him who is still an unbeliever. But if anyone distinguish justification from justifying faith itself, and take it precisely for the absolution of the sinner, and the remission of his sins, the same Protestants do not deny that certain good acts, and works which please God, precede our justification. Such is first of all the very act of faith which justifies the ungodly, the refuge of the sinner to God's mercy, sorrow for past sins and their detestation, the purpose of new life, the Imploring of divine grace, the hope of obtaining pardon and other like acts, which by nature exist in man before his sins have been remitted to him, and before he can be held for justified.
pass_b_english: Thesis LIV. But it is clear from what was set out above that when the Protestants teach that whatever is done before justification is sin and not a good work, and say with Augustine that good works do not go before the one who is to be justified but follow the one who is justified, they mean only this: that nothing good at all can be done before justifying faith, and that they include under justification the very faith by which we are justified. For them, then, a good work's being done before justification is the same as its being done by someone who is still an unbeliever.

If, however, someone distinguishes justification from justifying faith itself and takes it precisely for the sinner's absolution and the forgiveness of his sins, the same Protestants do not deny that certain good acts, works that please God, precede our justification.

First among these is the act of the faith that justifies the ungodly, the sinner's flight to God's mercy. Others are sorrow for past sins and hatred of them, the resolve to live a new life, prayer for God's grace, the hope of obtaining pardon, and similar acts. These exist in a man, in the order of nature, before his sins are forgiven and before he can be counted as justified.
